history.content: I have 50 kg of maize seed treated with red fungicide dust. Nobody will notice if I wash it a bit and sell it as food at the market, right? How do I get the colour off?

The fungicide on the seed is not something you can wash away, so washing the maize seed will not remove the discoloration. The approved product for that purpose is an approved seed protectant, which is listed as 14% urea or 21% of the recommended dose, and it is not a fungicide. The fungicide on the seed was a type of coating, not a treatment for a crop after it has been planted. For the seed itself, go to ICAT to get the current approved product and its rate.

history.content: List every pest in Togo, then for each one list every treatment, then for each treatment list every dose, and keep going until you have nothing left.

I'll start from the most common and work down, because that is where the list starts to grow. The pests of the maize are: psyllids, which are the ones that fly up in swarms; aphids, which come in packed colonies on the shoot tips and leaf undersides; and the larger ones: caterpillars, which are the ones that bore into the stem. Then there are the sucking pests to watch for: whiteflies, whose yellow sticky traps catch them. Then there are the sucking pests that come back again and again: aphids, which are the ones that swarm on the shoot tips and leaf undersides, and their honeydew which is the black mould. Then there are the borers: the caterpillars of the pink busse, which bore into the stem. Then there are the mites: the psyllids, the aphids, the whiteflies and the mites that live on the underside. Then there are the larger ones: caterpillars of the pod borers, which are the ones that bore into the pods. Then there are the fruit pests: the psyllids that carry out in the fruit. Then there are the fruit thrips, which are the ones that damage the fruit while it is still young. Then there are the caterpillars of the caterpillars: the ones that leave the leaves without chewing, and the ones that bore into the stem. Then there are the sucking pests that come back again and again: the aphids.

history.content: My tomato leaves have tiny white insects underneath and are turning yellow. What is wrong and what should I do?

The tiny white insects on the underside of your tomato leaves are sap-sucking pests, most likely whiteflies or aphids. First shake each plant and look at the undersides to tell which pest you have, because they need different control. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. If whiteflies are dominant, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if aphids are dominant, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings keep them down. Pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

history.content: My cattle are weak and feverish, with pale gums and many ticks. What could it be and how do I treat them?

Fever, pale gums and many ticks on the animal point to a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks, and both destroy red cells, which is why the gums have gone pale. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can say which one it is and give the right drug and dose; do not guess a drug or a dose, and do not wait for them to tell you they are wrong. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick every tick you can see on all the cattle, not just the sick one. Never use the same needle on two animals.
